entry.title: From External Service to Field Execution: Crowd Workforce Integration in SAP S/4HANA and SAP FSA
entry.content:
Crowd Integration Between S/4HANA and FSA

Business Context

If your organisation uses SAP S/4HANA for service management and SAP Field Service and Asset (FSA) for field execution, you've likely hit this wall: your external contractors exist in both systems, but those systems have never talked to each other about them. Every external service item in a service scenario required someone to manually create a matching activity in FSA. Every purchase order got created by a procurement person acting on an email. Every timesheet required a manual service confirmation entry in S/4HANA. On the FSA side, the dispatcher had no visibility of the lean service order at all. Every external service item requires someone to manually create a matching activity in FSA, attach the right reference, and keep it in sync with S/4HANA. The lean service process and the field execution process ran in parallel — connected only by people making phone calls and sending emails between them. The integration was you.

As of the 2025 FPS02 release, that changes. The Crowd Workforce Integration is now a standard feature of the S/4HANA–FSA product landscape, delivered through the existing standard Cloud Integration package. It keeps the master data in sync automatically — suppliers and their technicians replicate from S/4HANA to FSA as Crowd Partners and Technicians without any manual intervention. And it wires the lean service procurement chain directly to FSA crowd workforce events — so the PO is created when the supplier accepts the work, the SES is created when the technician logs their time, and the confirmation follows automatically. This post explains what problem it solves, what it delivers, and how it works end to end.

Blog Series:

Part 1: Crowd Integration Between S/4HANA and FSA -- Business Context, Solution Architecture, How it Works

Part 2: Make It Work: Configuring Crowd Integration Across S/4HANA and FSA

The Problem in Plain Terms

Field service operations that rely on external contractors — subcontractors, specialist partners, crowd workforce networks — sit at the intersection of two SAP platforms. S/4HANA owns the service order, the procurement chain, and the financials. FSA owns the dispatching, the Partner Portal, and the mobile execution. Before this integration, the two systems simply didn't know what each other was doing with the external workforce.

Here are the five gaps that teams were bridging manually every day:

Duplicate master data with no sync Suppliers and their technicians (Service Performers) lived in S/4HANA. The same people — modelled as crowd partners and technicians in FSA — had to be maintained separately in FSA. No link. No sync. When a new technician joined a supplier, someone updated S/4HANA and then manually created the same person in FSA. When someone left, both systems needed updating independently.

External service items invisible to FSA dispatchers When a service manager created a service order with an external service item (SREW/SRVW), FSA saw nothing. A dispatcher couldn't assign it because it didn't exist in their system. Someone had to manually create an FSA activity, attach the right reference, and keep it in sync with the S/4HANA item. With any volume of external work, this became a daily overhead.

No feedback from FSA back into S/4HANA Who accepted the assignment? When did field execution start? Which technician actually did the work? S/4HANA had no answers to these questions because FSA had no way to push that information back. The service order item sat with no visibility of its real-world status until someone manually updated it.

Purchase orders created by hand at the wrong time The lean service procurement chain — Purchase Requisition, Purchase Order, Service Entry Sheet, Service Confirmation — is a financial control process. The PO should be created when a supplier actually commits to doing the work, not before and not days after. Without integration, POs were created manually based on phone calls or emails, often at the wrong moment, and with no automated link to the underlying activity.

Timesheets disconnected from financial postings When a technician finished work and logged time in the FSA mobile app, that information had to travel by email or paper to a finance user who then manually created a service confirmation in S/4HANA. Month-end closings turned into reconciliation exercises. Errors were common. The gap between actual cost and recognised cost could span days or weeks.

 What the Integration Delivers

The integration closes all five gaps. Here's the direct outcome for each:

Gap

Solution

Duplicate master data

Supplier BPs and service performers in S/4HANA replicate automatically to FSA as Crowd Partners and Technicians. Incremental changes sync — new technicians added, deactivated technicians inactivated.

External items invisible to FSA

On service order release, the external service item is automatically created in FSA as an activity with subtype 'External Item' and a full reference back to the S/4HANA documents.

No FSA-to-S/4HANA feedback

Assignment acceptance and activity release events push status and parties (vendor, service performer) back into the S/4HANA service order automatically.

Manual PO creation

The Purchase Order is created automatically when the crowd partner releases the activity for execution — zero manual intervention via the FSMIMPORT technical user.

Manual service confirmation

Time effort approval in FSA triggers automatic Service Entry Sheet creation and approval in S/4HANA, which triggers the Service Confirmation. Real-time cost capture.

 

How It Works: Master Data

The master data half of the integration is straightforward: it maps S/4HANA business partner structures to FSA crowd workforce structures. The key building block is the Supplier Business Partner with service performer relationships.

Crowd Workforce sync

In S/4HANA, a vendor who provides field service workers is modelled as a Business Partner with the Supplier (FLVN01) role. That supplier can have employees related to them through the BUR025 relationship type using partner function BBP005 — the Service Performer partner function, which becomes available when Business Function /SHCM/EE_BP_1 is activated. These employees are created with both Employee and Contingent Worker person types so that their Business Partner record carries both the Employee role and the Service Performer role.

When this structure is in place and the integration is active, the new Crowd Partner interface replicates it to FSA as follows:

S/4HANA Object

FSA Object

Business Partner — Supplier role (FLVN01)

Crowd Partner (company entity in FSA Crowd Workforce)

Employee BP with Service Performer role (on relationship with Supplier)

Crowd Admin/Technician

 Replication is event-driven and incremental. Adding a new service performer to a supplier creates a new Crowd Technician in FSA. Removing the relationship deactivates them. The customer doesn't need to touch FSA for any of this — S/4HANA is the single source of truth.

There's also a variant — where the supplier wants to manage their own technicians in FSA without replicating them from S/4HANA. In that case, only the Crowd Partner is created from the S/4HANA supplier. The technicians are added directly in FSA by the crowd partner admin. Part 2 of this series covers how to configure each variant.

How It Works: The Transaction Flow

Here's the complete end-to-end flow once master data is in place.

Service Transactional in conjunction with SAP FSA 

  1. S/4HANA — Service manager creates a service order in S/4HANA with one or more External Service Items (item category SRVW). These items represent work to be executed by an external supplier.
  2. S/4HANA — On Release — Service manager releases the service order. Two things happen automatically in parallel: S/4HANA creates a Purchase Requisition for the external service item (standard lean service procurement), and the CPI iFlow sends the service order and item to FSA.
  3. FSA —Service Call and an Activity for the external service item created. The activity carries subtype ‘External Service’ and an ExternalId in the format <ServiceOrder>/<Item>/<PurchaseRequisition>_<PRItem> — making the full procurement reference traceable directly from the FSA dispatching board.
  4. FSA — Dispatching Board — The FSA dispatcher opens the dispatching board, finds the new activity (filtered by service order or subtype 'External Service'), and assigns it to an available external resource (crowd resource) — one of the technicians replicated from the relevant supplier.
  5. FSA Partner Portal — S/4HANA update — Automatic — The crowd admin logs into the Crowd Partner Portal and accepts the assignment. On acceptance, the crowd.activity.accepted event is emitted and the Notify Service Order iFlow updates the S/4HANA service order with the Vendor Party as supplier. Once the Crowd admin assigns Activity to a technician the Service Performer will be populated as the assigned technician.
  6. FSA Partner Portal — The crowd admin releases the activity for field execution, this is the moment that triggers the crowd.activity.released business event to create a Purchase Order against the existing Purchase Requisition in S/4HANA. The service order item execution status changes to 'In Execution'. No manual procurement needed. For traceability, the Activity ExternalId is updated as <ServiceOrder>/<Item>/<PurchaseRequisition>_<PRItem>/<PurchaseOrder>_<POItem>
  7. FSA Mobile App — The technician executes the work and logs time effort in the FSA mobile app via the EMME (Efforts, Materials, Mileage, Expenses) journal.
  8. FSA Partner Portal or FSA TimeApprovals— The crowd admin reviews and approves the time effort in FSA.
  9. S/4HANA —On approval of the time effort, a Service Entry Sheet in S/4HANA referring to the Purchase Order created in step 6. The SES is automatically approved by the standard interface.
  10. S/4HANA — S/4HANA automatically creates a Service Confirmation on SES approval. Actual cost is recognised against the service order. No manual posting required.
  11. FSA/S/4HANA — Existing Process — Non-time EMME entries like materials, mileage & other expenses — follow the existing standard FSA service confirmation flow. No change to that path.

See It In Action

Here is the E2E demo video of automated service scenario between S/4HANA & FSA:

 

What Gets Created Automatically: The Document Chain

To make the automation concrete — here's every document that gets created without a human touching it, and the trigger for each:

Document

Created When

Created By

Purchase Requisition

Service Order Release

S/4HANA lean service procurement (standard)

FSA Service Call

Service Order Release

CPI: Replicate Service Order iFlow

FSA Activity (Ext. Item)

Service Order Release

CPI: Replicate Service Order iFlow

Purchase Order

crowd.activity.released event in FSA

CPI: Route Payload iFlow → New Notify Crowd update interface

Service Entry Sheet

EMME time effort approved in FSA

CPI: Route Payload iFlow → New Service Entry Sheet interface

Service Confirmation

SES auto-approval

S/4HANA standard (on SES approval)

 The External Service item is updated with all other crowd business events like below:

FSM Crowd Business Event

S/4HANA Action

crowd.activity.accepted & confirmed

Vendor Party updated & Executing Service Employee on the Ext. Service Item

crowd.activity.assigned

Service Performer Party is updated with assigned crowd technician

crowd.activity.released

Status of the Ext. Service Item is set to “In Execution” and Purchase Order is created referencing the PR.

crowd.activity.handedover

Update Service Performer with the new technician details

crowd.activity.cancelled

Delete the PO and remove the Service Performer

crowd.activity.replanned

Update Executing Service Employee and Service Performer

crowd.activity.unassigned

Delete PO, remove Service Performer and Executing Performer

  Availability

The Crowd Workforce Integration is a standard, supported feature as of SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud 2025 FPS02. It does not require a separate connector licence or custom development — it extends the existing SAP S/4HANA to SAP FSA integration package delivered through SAP BTP Integration Suite. If you already have the standard S/4HANA–FSA integration running, you're building on the same infrastructure.

 

Up next: Part 2 - Step by Step guide to activate the Crowd Integration between S/4HANA and FSA

entry.title: New features in the Pipeline for Cloud Integration packages with the Oct 2026 shipment
entry.content:
We have just shipped new versions of the Pipeline for Cloud Integration packages. Those include couple of feature enhancements but also fixes that were reported.

The following new versions have been shipped:

  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Inbound version 1.0.9
  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Pipelines version 1.0.7
  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Outbound version 1.1.1
  • Cloud Integration Pipeline - Templates version 1.2.1

Here the list of new features at a glance:

  • New generic XI and IDoc outbound processing flows on Edge Integration Cell: Two new integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI on Edge" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc on Edge" have been added to the Cloud Integration Pipeline - Generic Outbound package. Deploy and run those flows on Edge Integration Cell if you need to handle XI and/or IDoc outbound scenarios when running the pipeline on Edge Integration Cell. Dedicated flows were needed because the adapter configuration with the proxy type On-Premise is not supported on Edge Integration Cell and hence the corresponding other flows for the Cloud Integration could not be deployed on Edge Integration Cell. For the new flows, currently the proxy type Internet is supported only. The proxy type Manual will be added with one of the next increments but here we depend on development. See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.
  • Exactly Once In Order routing for XI and IDoc inbound processing: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step01 - Inbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step01 - Inbound Processing for Idoc" now support the handling of messages when sent with Quality of Service Exactly Once In Order (EOIO). The approach is to forward EOIO messages to an integration flow whereas you bypass most of the pipeline steps. So, this approach would unblock you as long as the pipeline does not support EOIO from end-to-end. And this way, you can use single point of entries for your XI and IDoc inbound scenarios regardless of the quality of service. You have the option to forward Exactly Once In Order messages either to an exclusive queue or to a ProcessDirect end point. See In Order Handling.
  • Generic XI and IDoc outbound processing flows supporting receiver with parties: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" now support receiver with party when configuring the XI and IDoc adapters in the Partner Directory. See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.
  • Additional option to override IDoc control record: The integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for IDoc" has been enhanced to be able to maintain the list of IDoc EDIDC control record fields to be overridden by configuring the externalized parameter OverrideControlRecordParameters. With this, you now have three options to maintain the override parameter: via message header in the scenario-specific flow, as string parameter in the Partner Directory, and as externalized parameter of the generic Idoc outbound flow. See IDoc Receiver Adapter.
  • Disable mandatory IDoc control record fields check: For the integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc", a new configuration parameter EnableControlRecordCheck has been introduced. By default, the parameter is true so that message processing fails if any mandatory control record field is empty or missing. This check has been introduced previously. With the new parameter, you now have the option to disable the check by setting the parameter value to false. In this case, empty mandatory control record fields are ignored and the message processing won't fail in Cloud Integration. You disable the check, when you rather check empty mandatory control record fields in the backend system. See IDoc Receiver Adapter.
  • Enhanced inbound conversion definition: Sender-specific inbound conversion now supports sender party to determine the endpoint of the scenario-specific inbound conversion flow. See Inbound Conversion.
  • Custom pre-processing for standard error handling: The standard error handling has been enhanced supporting custom pre-processing. You now have the option to call a pre-processing custom error flow before calling the standard error handling. Before, it was only possible to replace the standard error handling with your own custom error handling logic. Now, you can stick to the standard error handling and call a custom flow right before the standard error handling is performed. A use case may be to automatically create an incident ticket if maximum number of retries have been exceeded. See Custom Exception Handling.
  • Custom post-processing: The integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step06 - Outbound Processing" now supports custom exits for post-processing. You have the options to call a custom flow after the message delivery to the next step across all scenarios or scenario-specific without the need to alter the standard flow provided. For latter, you can maintain the string parameters CustomXPostEnabled and CustomXPostEndpoint, repectively, in the Partner Directory. Right now, the CustomXPostEnabled only supports step number 06. See Custom Postprocessing Exit.
  • Custom pre-transmission: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" now support custom exits for pre-transmission. You have the options to call a custom flow right before the message delivery to the receiving system across all scenarios or scenario-specific without the need to alter the standard flows provided. In addition to the header customXPipelineStep (in this case equals 08), the header customXProtocol (either xi or idoc) is passed to the custom exit flow. See Custom Preprocessing and Pretransmission Exit.
  • Enhanced custom pre-processing setting: The scenario-specific custom exit definition has been enhanced. For each pipeline step, you can now define an own end point by adding the pipeline step number as suffix to the string parameter CustomXPreEndpoint in the Partner Directory. See Custom Preprocessing and Pretransmission Exit.
  • Enhanced allowed headers for custom error handling template: For the "Pipeline v2 Template - Custom Error Handling" template, the allowed headers has been enhanced by adding the regular expression "customX(.*)".
  • Enhanced custom exit template: For the "Pipeline v2 Template - Custom Exit" template, an additional route has been added to support the pipeline step number 08.
  • Supporting slash (/) in sender interface: The integration flow "Pipeline v2 Generic Step01 - Inbound Processing for XI" now supports slash (/) in the sender interface name when using a combination of sender, sender interface and sender interface namespace to determine the partner ID. For the combination of sender and sender interface with fixed ID "SenderInterface", slash (/) was supported before anyway. See Partner ID.
  • Supporting slash (/) in receiver interface: The integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" now support slash (/) in the interface name. When maintaining the configuration parameters in the Partner Directory, the slash (/) needs to be replaced by underscore (_). See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.

The following fixes have been provided:

  • Harden max retry condition: For the "Pipeline v2 Generic Step06 - Outbound Processing" flow, the max retry handling condition was slightly adapted to be more robust avoiding endless message retry. Instead of using equal (=) in the condition, we now use greater or equal than (>=).
  • Type conversion issue: We fixed a bug which resulted into a type conversion exception when in an error case an original message in XML format was stored in the dead letter queue. This happened only for cases where the original XML message was converted into a non-XML message like JSON for instance. The fix was implemented in the restoreMessage script.
  • Wrong condition: We fixed a bug in the integration flows "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for XI" and "Pipeline v2 Generic Step08 - Outbound Processing for Idoc" with the complex conditions evaluations to route to the corresponding receiver adapters. The condition was hence replaced by a groovy script.

Please update the packages in your Design area to benefit from the changes. We recommend to update your dev and test landscape first and to test there before updating the content on your prod tenant. Though we run extensive regression tests and new feature tests before publishing a new version.

entry.title: Make It Work: Configuring Crowd Integration Across SAP S/4HANA and SAP FSA
entry.content:
This post is for the consultants and administrators who are actually setting up the Crowd Workforce Integration between SAP S/4HANA and SAP FSA. Part 1 of this series covered the business problem and how the integration works end to end. Here we get into the specifics: what to configure, in which system, in what order, and what to check when you're done.

Blog Series:

Part 1: Crowd Integration Between S/4HANA and FSA -- Business Context, Solution Architecture, How it Works

Part 2: Make It Work: Configuring Crowd Integration Across S/4HANA and FSA

We cover two deployment scenarios. Scenario A is the standard setup where technicians are replicated from S/4HANA service performers. Scenario B is the variant — used when the crowd partner wants to manage their own technicians directly in FSA without a corresponding employee record in S/4HANA.

Prerequisites at a Glance

System

Object / Setting

Action

Why It Matters

SAP S/4HANA

Business Function /SHCM/EE_BP_1

Activate in Switch Framework (transaction SFW5)

Enables the Service Performer partner function BBP005 and BUR025 relationship type for Business Partners while converting the Employee to Business Partner

SAP S/4HANA

SAP Note 0002882172

Review and apply as required

Documents known issues and corrections related to the /SHCM/EE_BP_1 Business Function activation

SAP S/4HANA

Item Category for External Service Item

SRVW (or SREW for returns) configured in service order customising

Identifies service order items as external — triggers PR creation and FSA activity with subtype 'External Service

SAP S/4HANA

Lean Service Procurement

Standard lean service integration between SM and MM configured

Required for automatic PR creation on service order release

SAP BTP / CPI

SAP S/4HANA–FSA integration package

Already deployed and active

Crowd integration extends the existing iFlows — it does not replace them

SAP FSA

Crowd Workforce module

Licensed and enabled in the FSA tenant

Required for Crowd Partner and Technician objects to exist in FSA

SAP FSA

Crowd Partner Portal

Enabled in FSA tenant configuration

External crowd partners need portal access for assignment acceptance and EMME approval

 Scenario A: Standard Setup — Technicians Replicated from S/4HANA

This is the default scenario. Everything flows from S/4HANA: the supplier, their workers, and all field activity assignments are traceable back to S/4HANA records. Use this when the customer wants S/4HANA as the single system of record for both the supplier relationship and the individual technicians.

Step 1 — Activate Business Function /SHCM/EE_BP_1

Go to transaction SFW5 in S/4HANA. Locate Business Function /SHCM/EE_BP_1 and activate it. This is a permanent, irreversible activation — confirm with the customer before proceeding. Once activated, it makes the following available:

  • Partner function BBP005 (Service Performer) for use in Business Partner relationships
  • Relationship type BUR025 (Employee — has Service Performer) between a person BP and a company BP
  • The person type 'Contingent Worker' on Employee BPs, which generates the Service Performer BP role on BP conversion

Important: Review SAP Note 0002882172 before activating. It covers known corrections for this Business Function that may apply to your release level.

If Customer uses Employee Group other than “9” for contingent worker than a BADi implementation is required. Reference blog: External Workforce in Employee Business Partner Data Model

 Use the synchronization reports (/SHCM/RH_SYNC_BUPA_EMPL_SINGLE or /SHCM/RH_SYNC_BUPA_FROM_EMPL), to sync created employees as Business Partner with role BUP003 and BBP005.

 Step 2 — Configure Partner Function BBP005 for Relationship Type BUR025

Create your supplier as a Business Partner (transaction FLVN01) with the relevant purchasing organisation and currency. Then link the service performers to this supplier using relationship type BUR025 — Has Service Performer.

That's the trigger. Once those relationships are saved, the new CPI iFlow — "Replicate Crowd Partner and Technician from SAP S/4HANA to SAP Field Service and Asset Management" — picks them up automatically and creates the Crowd Partner and Crowd Technicians in FSA. Adding or removing service performers later is handled the same way — the changes flow through to FSA Crowd Workforce without any manual intervention.

One thing that must be in place before replication runs: make sure a valid address dependent email is maintained on both the Supplier BP and each Employee BP. FSA requires an email address to create Crowd Partner and Technician records — it's how the platform sends onboarding notifications to the crowd partner. Missing emails will stop the replication.

If you don't want to maintain individual technicians in S/4HANA, there's a configuration option for that. Set the iFlow external parameter “CrowdPartner W/O Service Performer” to true. In this mode, the supplier replicates to FSA as a Crowd Partner with a placeholder technician carrying the supplier's details. The crowd partner admin then manages their own technicians directly in FSA. This is the right choice when the customer wants to keep their external workforce data out of S/4HANA entirely.

Role Mapping: Crowd Admin vs Crowd Technician: employees created with both Employee and Contingent Worker person types get both the Crowd Admins roles in FSA.

Step 3 — Configure Item Category for External Service Items

In Customizing path “SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Transactions -> Basic Settings -> Define Item Category Determination”, ensure the item category SRVW and SREW are configured and assigned to the relevant order type (SRVO) and item category group (SRVP or DIEN).

With this you can add External Service item categories to the Service Order.

In Customer path “SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Transactions  Settings for Service Transactions -> Integration -> Logistics Integration -> Enterprise Organizational Management -> Define Logistics Scenario for Procurement of Materials and Services”, for the Purchase Requisition to auto create on the External Service Item, add PREQ as logistic.

If you are using legacy org, then patch will “SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Transactions  Settings for Service Transactions -> Integration -> Logistics Integration -> Organizational Management(Legacy) -> Define Logistics Scenario for Procurement of Materials and Services”

Step 4 — Add Vendor and Service Performer Parties in Service

To update the Vendor and External technician to the External service item, maintain Vendor (0000019) and Service Performer (0000028) functions against Ext. Service Item (00000032) & Ext. Confirmation Service Item (00000033) categories in the Partner Function determination in Service.

Customizing path: “SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Service -> Basic Functions -> Partner Processing -> Define Partner Determination Procedure in Service”

Step 5: Authorization to access Purchase apps:

Make sure you have below roles to view purchase orders, requisition and service entry sheet

SAP_BR_EMPLOYEE_PROCUREMENT, SAP_BR_PURCHASER. SAP_BR_INTERNAL_SALES_REP

Step 6: Maintain Purchasing Info Record:

Maintain mapping of Purchase Org and Plant with the Service Material and Supplier in Purchasing Info Record (tcode ME11). This is required to create purchase order using purchase requisition.

Step 7 — Configure the CPI iFlows

In SAP BTP Integration Suite, open the standard package “SAP S/4HANA Integration with SAP Field Service and Assent Management”. The four iFlows relevant to crowd integration are:

  • Replicate Service Order from SAP S4HANA to SAP Field Service and Asset Management SOAP — sends service order and external service item to FSA on release. Configure “External Service Item Categories” as SRVW,SREW.
  • Notify External Service Order Item with Crowd Changes from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA – sends all crowd updates to external item.
  • Crowd Service Entry Sheet Creation from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA – creates Service Entry Sheet on activity confirmations on external activity.
  • Route Payload from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S/4HANA — handles all inbound FSA crowd events

Step 8 —FSA Connector Events for Crowd Business Events

The crowd business events mentioned below will be routed through the FSM Connector outbound event to initiate CPI endpoint. There is not configuration required, this will be taken care by standard in FSA.

Event

When It Fires

What It Triggers in S/4HANA

crowd.activity.assigned and accepted

Crowd partner accepts assignment in Partner Portal

Updates Vendor and Service Performer on S/4HANA service order item

crowd.activity.released

Crowd partner releases activity for field execution

Triggers automatic PO creation in S/4HANA via FSMIMPORT

crowd.activity.cancelled

Assignment cancelled by crowd partner

Updates service order status in S/4HANA

crowd.activity.unassigned

Activity unassigned from crowd resource

Clears assignment data from S/4HANA service order item

EMME time effort approved

activity.confirmed on external activity

Crowd admin approves time effort booking

Creates SES (for time effort) + auto-approves + triggers Service Confirmation in S/4HANA

Create Service Confirmations for other non-time EMME’s like Expenses, Mileages, & Material

 Step 9 — Enable the Crowd Workforce Module in FSA

In FSA, go to Admin → Company Settings and verify that the Crowd module is enabled.

For details, refer to Configure Single Tenant Crowd.

Scenario B - Technicians Managed Only in FSA

Some customers want to onboard their external suppliers as crowd partners in FSA but don't want to maintain individual technician records in S/4HANA. The supplier manages their own workforce directly in FSA.

To achieve this, follow below handling in the configurations:

In the CPI iFlow parameters, configure “CrowdPartner W/O Service Performer” parameter as true in below iflows

  • Replicate Business Partner
  • Replicate Crowd Partner and Technician from SAP S4HANA to SAP Field Service and Asset Management
  • Crowd Service Entry Sheet Creation from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA
  • Notify External Service Order Item with Crowd Changes from SAP Field Service and Asset Management to SAP S4HANA

 The effects of that single flag change:

  • The Supplier BP still replicates to FSA as a Crowd Partner — the company-level entity is created
  • No Crowd Technicians or Admins are created from S/4HANA service performer relationships
  • The crowd partner admin creates and manages their own technicians directly in FSA
  • When the crowd partner accepts and releases assignments, S/4HANA receives the status update (In Execution) but not the Executing Service Employee nor Service Performer.

 Note that email is maintained on the Supplier in this scenario as well.

Scenario Comparison

Capability

Scenario A — Standard

Scenario B — Without Technician S4HANA

Technician data in S/4HANA

Required (employee BPs with BUR025 relationship)

Not required

Crowd Technician creation

Automatic from S/4HANA service performer replication

Manual, directly in FSA by crowd partner admin

Technician identity in S/4HANA

Visible on service order Parties Involved

Not populated (status update only)

Executing Employee on Confirmation

Actual technician from FSA assignment

Fallback to service order creator

Best for

Customers who manage supplier workforce in S/4HANA and want full traceability

Customers who let suppliers self-manage their teams in FSA

 EMME Processing: Two Paths, One Clear Rule

When a technician books work through the FSA EMME journal, the integration handles different entry types differently. This is worth understanding explicitly because it affects what gets created in S/4HANA.

Path A: Time Efforts

Time effort entries — the hours a technician spent on the job — go through a specific path that uses the Purchase Order created earlier in the process:

  1. Technician logs time effort in FSA mobile app
  2. Crowd admin approves the time effort
  3. CPI iFlow creates a Service Entry Sheet in S/4HANA referencing the Purchase Order
  4. The SES is automatically approved by the integration
  5. S/4HANA creates a Service Confirmation on SES approval — actual cost is posted

The SES → Confirmation path is what makes this integration financially compliant. The Purchase Order acts as the financial commitment, the SES captures the actual delivery, and the Confirmation posts the cost. This is the standard three-way match for service procurement.

Path B: Materials, Mileage, and Expenses

Non-time EMME entries — materials used, mileage driven, expenses incurred — follow the existing standard FSA service confirmation flow. There is no change to this path. These entries do not go through the SES route and are not tied to the Purchase Order. They create service confirmations directly in S/4HANA through the same mechanism that was already in place before the crowd integration.

Worth Clarifying with Customers: If your customer uses material items heavily in their EMME journals, make sure they understand that only time efforts go through the SES path. Material-based costs are confirmed separately and are not linked to the crowd PO.

entry.title: CISTEPS 1.0.0 Beta — Smart Editing, Governance and Dependency Tracing for SAP Cloud Integration
entry.content:
Maintaining an SAP Cloud Integration iFlow can become difficult very quickly.

As integrations grow, developers often need to reorganize layouts, understand unfamiliar flows, review technical naming, and discover where Headers and Properties are being used.

That is the idea behind CISTEPS — Cloud Integration Smart Steps.

CISTEPS 1.0.0 Beta — Smart Editing and Inspection for SAP Cloud Integration

Maintaining a large SAP Cloud Integration iFlow can become difficult very quickly.

Developers often need to reorganize layouts, review technical naming, and understand where Headers and Properties are being used.

That is the idea behind CISTEPS — Cloud Integration Smart Steps.

CISTEPS is an independent community browser extension designed to support developers directly inside the iFlow editor.

It focuses on three areas:

  • Smart Edit
  • Governance Scan
  • Dependency Tracing

CISTEPS 1.0.0 is currently released as a Beta.

How to Use CISTEPS

The simplest way to use CISTEPS is directly inside the iFlow editor.

  1. Hold the Alt key on your keyboard.
  2. Click the activity where you want to create or reduce space.
  3. Choose Expand or Compact.
  4. Enter the number of pixels you want to move.
  5. Preview the movement before applying it.
  6. If needed, use Undo to revert the change or clear the current selection and start again.

CISTEPS automatically determines the movement direction from the existing iFlow structure, so the same workflow can be used whether you need space horizontally or vertically.

The developer remains in control of how much space is created.

CISTEPS at a Glance

CISTEPS provides two workspaces:

Edit
For controlled layout adjustments.

Inspect
For governance checks and dependency analysis.

The goal is not to replace the SAP editor, but to simplify repetitive maintenance tasks.

1. Smart Edit

Sometimes the problem is very simple:

You need more space inside an iFlow.

Instead of manually moving several activities, CISTEPS allows you to select a step and Expand or Compact the surrounding layout.

Just need to select the element and hold button ALT

The extension follows the existing process structure and preserves:

  • branches
  • Local Processes
  • End Events
  • Request Reply / Send relationships
  • external receiver alignment

 

Without clean spaces:

With spaces:

It also provides:

  • Movement Preview
  • Undo
  • direction-aware movement

Select a step → Expand → show downstream movement → Undo.

2. Governance Scan

Large iFlows often contain technical names such as:

Content Modifier 3

Request Reply 4

Groovy Script 1

Router 2

These names work technically, but they make future maintenance harder.

CISTEPS Governance Scan identifies generic technical names and highlights them directly in the iFlow.

Where enough context exists, CISTEPS may also provide a naming suggestion.

The suggestion is only advisory.

CISTEPS does not rename components automatically or enforce a naming convention.

 

For large iFlows, Governance rendering is optimized to avoid continuously redrawing every finding on the canvas.

Run Governance → click a finding → show the corresponding component highlighted.

3. Header and Property Dependencies

When maintaining an unfamiliar iFlow, one common question is:

Where is this Property used?

A Header or Property may be referenced in different places:

  • Router conditions
  • Content Modifiers
  • adapters
  • Groovy
  • JavaScript
  • XSLT
  • Camel expressions

CISTEPS Dependency Scan tries to identify these relationships automatically.

For example:

Property: EmployeeIDs

may be referenced by:

Router: EmployeeID

and:

Adapter: SuccessFactors

Clicking the Property highlights its detected usages in the iFlow.

For Router conditions, CISTEPS can also identify the related branch and place the marker directly on that Sequence Flow.

Example:

${property.EmployeeIDs} != ''

can be connected to:

Property: EmployeeIDs

Run Dependencies → click EmployeeIDs → click Router usage → show the branch marker.

Script and XSLT Analysis

Dependency tracing also includes available development resources such as:

  • Groovy
  • JavaScript
  • XSLT

For example:

message.getProperty("EmployeeIDs")

or:

message.getHeader("CorrelationID")

can be associated with the related Header or Property.

The goal is not to create a full static-code-analysis engine.

The goal is to give developers useful maintenance context.

When CISTEPS cannot reliably prove a relationship, it should not invent one.

Context Handling

When moving from one iFlow to another, CISTEPS automatically resets the previous context.

This includes:

  • selections
  • Governance findings
  • Dependency markers
  • script/resource cache
  • Preview state
  • Undo history

This avoids mixing information between different integration flows.

Availability

Chrome Web Store:
Chrome WebStore - CISTEPS 

Version:
1.0.0 Beta

Disclaimer

CISTEPS is an independent community project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by SAP.

It relies on SAP Cloud Integration editor internals, which may change over time.

No iFlow data is transmitted by the extension.

Closing

CISTEPS started from a very simple idea:

How can I open space inside an iFlow without manually moving everything?

It now also helps answer:

Where is this Property used?

Which Router branch depends on it?

Are these technical names helping future maintenance?

The goal remains simple:

reduce repetitive work and make iFlow maintenance easier.

Thank you.

entry.title: Best Practices Pipeline for Cloud Integration: How to deal with slash in the interface name
entry.content:
In the latest announcement New features in the Pipeline for Cloud Integration packages with the Oct 2026 shipment about the new Pipeline for Cloud Integration version, you may have seen that we added further support for slash (/) in the interface name and you may wonder what this is all about.

Well, there are some character restrictions of the Partner Directory that we heavily use to dynamically configure the configuration scenarios for messages running through the pipeline. For some use cases, you need to enter the interface name into an alternative partner or for defining a string parameter. The scheme of an alternative partner and the ID of a string parameter do not support special characters such as slash (/). Hence, the issue occurs if your interface name contains a slash (/) which is not so uncommon when exchanging IDoc messages for instance.

The general approach to overcome this restriction is to replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_) if you configure Partner Directory fields that do not support the special characters. During message processing, your interface name can contain special characters. However, to read the Partner Directory string parameters or to determine your partner ID, the special characters are automatically replaced with an underscore (_) in the flow scripts and can therefore be matched with the Partner Directory settings.

Note, that the value of a string parameter and the ID of an alternative partner do support slash (/). So, here you must not replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_).

What are the use cases where this approach needs to be applied?

  • For incoming messages, we need to determine the partner ID based on an alternative partner. In most cases, the sender system name and the sender interface name is sufficient to unambiguously determine the partner ID. In this case, we use a constant term for the Scheme of the alternative partner and hence won't be impacted by the character restriction. However, if the combination of sender system name and sender interface name alone is not sufficient and it becomes unambiguous only together with the sender interface namespace, then the Scheme of your alternative partner needs to hold the sender interface name. If now your sender interface name contains a slash (/), then this needs to be replaced with an underscore (_). See Partner ID.
  • For outgoing messages using either the generic XI outbound processing flow or the generic IDoc outbound processing flow, you have the option to configure the XI/IDoc connection parameters and the scenario parameters using the Partner Directory. Here, for some of your settings the string parameters may contain the receiver interface name. If now your receiver interface name contains a slash (/), then this needs to be replaced with an underscore (_). See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.

Inbound use case where slash (/) must not be replaced

If possible, define the alternative partner as a combination of the sender system name and the sender interface name. In this case, the alternative partner is defined as follows:

  • Agency holds the sender system name
  • Scheme is constant "SenderInterface"
  • ID equals the sender interface name

As you can see, for this option we must not replace the slash (/) of the sender interface name because the ID of the alternative partner supports special characters.

Inbound use case where slash (/) needs to be replaced

If you need the sender interface namespace to make the key unambiguous, you need to define the alternative partner as follows:

  • Agency holds the sender system name
  • Scheme equals the sender interface name
  • ID equals the sender interface namespace

As you can see, for this option you must replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_) when maintaining the Scheme. In our case, the sender interface name is actually /SI_PurchaseOrder/Create/Outbound/Async. I have to admit that for test purposes, this name is a bit constructed. But a real customer case is to use the XI adapter to exchange IDoc messages that contain a slash (/)  in the IDoc type and message type.

If you run the scenario, you can see in the message monitoring that the sender interface name contains couple of slashes (/). During message processing the slashes (/) were replaced with underscore (_),  and the partner ID was successfully identified.

Outbound use case where slash (/) needs to be replaced

To configure the XI or IDoc outbound, you have three options: via message headers in the scenario-specific flow, via externalized parameters of the generic XI/IDoc outbound processing flow or via configuration in the Partner Directory. For latter option, if your receiver interface name contains a slash (/) and the string parameter ID requires to add the receiver interface name as suffix, you need to replace the slash (/) with an underscore (_).

In below example, we configure the IDoc outbound. Here, we like to override the control header parameters RCVPOR, RCVPRN, SNDPOR, and SNDPRN for the receiver interface /FLIGHTBOOK_CREATE./FLIGHTBOOK_CREATE01. When we add the receiver interface name as suffix, the slash (/) needs to be replaced.

If you run the scenario, you can see in the message monitoring that the control headers have been properly defined and the outbound processing has been successfully completed.

For a complete list of parameters for the generic IDoc outbound processing flow, see IDoc Receiver Adapter. For the generic XI outbound processing flow, see XI Receiver Adapter.

entry.title: Best Practices Pipeline for Cloud Integration: Working with Parties
entry.content:
You like to use parties in combination with the Pipeline for Cloud Integration. Parties need to be taken into consideration for different use cases and configuration options. So, this blog post describes how to generally setup your configuration scenarios when using parties.

Note: For exchanging IDoc messages, parties are heavily used when your partner type is not LS. Covering IDocs would exceed the scope of this blog post. For this, I would refer to Enhanced IDoc inbound support for Cloud Integration Pipeline where I describe how to setup IDoc inbound scenarios depending on the sender and (virtual) receiver partner type.

So, let's stick here to the more generic usage of parties. In general, we decided to go for a simplified way how to support parties in the Pipeline for Cloud Integration. We simply combine the party name and  the system name by separating both parts using a period, ".", e.g., PartyA.XYZ. See Scenarios with Sender Party or Receiver Party.

The combined party and system can then be used in different configurations such as:

  • In your alternative partner to determine the partner ID representing the configuration scenario.
  • For sender-specific inbound conversion.
  • In the XSLT to determine the receivers (with party).
  • For P2P, to determine the receiver (with party).
  • For the generic XI/IDoc outbound processing, to define the XI/IDoc connection and scenario settings.

So, here some rules:

  • In your scenario-specific integration flow, maintain the header SAP_Sender as combined sender party and sender system name as described above.
  • For XI inbound scenarios, this is automatically done. Here, the generic XI inbound processing flow creates the header SAP_Sender as a combination of the header SapSenderParty and SapSenderService provided by the XI sender adapter.
  • To determine the configuration scenario, maintain the alternative partner of the partner ID in the Partner Directory accordingly. In this case, define the agency as the combined sender party and sender system name.
  • For receiver parties, maintain the receiver service name in the XSLT to determine the receivers as combined receiver party and receiver system name.
  • For the Point-to-Point pattern, maintain the value of the string parameter receiverDetermination as combined receiver party and receiver system name.
  • For some configuration options, you need to add the combined party name and system name as suffix to the corresponding string parameter.

In message monitoring, you will notice the following:

  • If the header SAP_Sender contains a party, the header SAP_SenderParty is created holding the party name. Furthermore, the value of the header SAP_Sender is split up defining the custom header properties SenderParty and SenderSystem, which are then displayed in the message processing log.
  • If the header SAP_Receiver contains a party, the header SAP_ReceiverParty is created holding the party name. Furthermore, the value of the header SAP_Receiver is split up defining the custom header properties ReceiverParty and ReceiverSystem, which are then displayed in the message processing log.

Let's take a look at some examples.

XI inbound scenario

In this use case, we focus on the inbound side. This is a scenario where we send XI messages to the pipeline whereas the XI header contains both party and system.

We use landscape staging, and would like to test our scenario on the QA landscape. First of all, we need to define a business system alias for the sender system, here BC_02D_S1. In the alternative partner of the alias, we map the actual business system name, here BS_02D_S1Q for the QA landscape, to the alias. We do the same for the second sender, here alias BC_02D_S2 with actual business system name BS_02D_S2Q.

As said, both senders have a party. So, in the alternative partner of the partner ID representing the configuration scenario, we need to define the agency as combination of the party name and the system alias name. In our case BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 and BuyerB.BC_02D_S2, respectively. Scheme of the alternative partner is the sender interface name, ID is the sender interface namespace.

An inbound conversion is needed after the message has been received by the pipeline. In our case, the inbound conversion should be sender-specific. So, for each of the sender we define a string parameter InboundConversionEndpoint with suffix as combined party and sender system alias, here InboundConversionEndpoint_BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 and InboundConversionEndpoint_BuyerB.BC_02D_S2, respectively. As value, we enter the ProcessDirect endpoint of the inbound conversion flows that carry out the conversion.

I switched on the trace for the generic XI inbound processing flow. In the trace, you can see the payload of the incoming message including XI header. So, here you can see that the XI header contains the sender party BuyerA and the sender service BS_02D_S1Q.

In the message monitoring, you can see that the SAP_Sender (Sender in the Properties) is a combination of the party and the business system name, here BuyerA.BS_02D_S1Q. The custom header properties show the sender alias, sender system and sender party information. During runtime, the sender system alias BC_02D_S1 is determined based on the sender business system name BS_02D_S1Q and the landscape stage QA (via the alternative parner of the system alias). The combined party and sender system alias BuyerA.BC_02D_S1 is then used to determine the configuration scenario (via the alternative parner of the configuration scenario). Once, the configuration scenario has been determined, the other parameters are read from the Partner Directory to dynamically define how the message processing behaves.

Configure XI/IDoc Outbound

In this use case, we focus on the outbound side. This is a scenario where we use the generic XI and IDoc outbound processing flows to configure the XI and IDoc receiver adapters and scenario parameters. Here, the receivers contain party.

Again, we use landscape staging. First of all, we need to define a business system alias for the receiver system, here BC_02L_R1. In the alternative partner of the alias, we map the actual business system name, here BS_02L_R1Q for the QA landscape, to the alias.

This is a content-based router pattern. So, we create an XSLT mapping to determine the receivers and upload it to the Binary Parameters of the configuration scenario with ID receiverDetermination.

The XSLT looks as follows. As you can see, we either route a message to the one party or the other. In our case for both parties, the system is the same. However, they can also differ. In our case, the service is defined as combined party and receiver system alias, so either PRTY_02L_Bronze.BC_02L_R1 or PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1. Note: in the XSLT we always use the alias, so we can use the same XSLT in each landscape stage.

To configure the XI and IDoc outbound, we support different options: either as message headers in the scenario-specific outbound processing flow, as externalized parameters for dedicated generic XI/Idoc outbound flows, or in the Partner Directory. See XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.

In our case, we use the Partner Directory option. For the Partner Directory option, some of the parameters can be configured for the partner ID representing the configuration scenario or for the partner ID representing the party. In the configuration scenario, you then need to add the combined party and system alias as well as the receiver interface name as suffix to the parameter, e.g., XIAuthenticationType_PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1_SI_PurchaseOrderCreatePD_IB_Async. For the parameter InterfaceNameDetermination, it's just the combined party and system alias, e.g., InterfaceNameDetermination_PRTY_02L_Copper.BC_02L_R1.

If you like to maintain party-specific parameters, create a new partner ID with name equals the party name, here PRTY_02L_Copper and PRTY_02L_Bronze. For the parties, you need to add the business system name and not the alias as suffix to the parameter, e.g., XIEndpoint_BS_02L_R1Q.

I switched on the trace for the generic XI outbound processing flow. In the trace, you can see the payload of the outgoing message including XI header. So, here you can see that the XI header contains the receiver party PRTY_02L_Copper and the receiver service BS_02L_R1Q.

To fetch the scenario and connection parameters both are read, the configuration scenario and the party. As you can see, the correct values were read and the message could be successful delivered.

XI/IDoc Outbound without staging

Now, let's check how you could configure XI and IDoc outbound without staging if this is not required. So, we distinguish between two parties but use a business component as receiver system. In this case, you do not need to define a business alias, you simply use the business component name in the configuration, here EDI.

For the party, we also add the business component as suffix to the parameter.

For a complete list of parameters that you can define in both the configuration scenario and the party, refer to XI Receiver Adapter and IDoc Receiver Adapter.

entry.title: Calling SAP SuccessFactors from Postman with OAuth 2.0 (SAML Bearer Assertion) - No External Tools
entry.content:
SAP SuccessFactors is retiring HTTP Basic Authentication (user and password) for its APIs. The retirement is planned for November 2026, and published sources give either 13 or 20 November, so the earlier date is the safer one to plan for. After that date, OData calls and SOAP calls such as CompoundEmployee will only accept token-based authentication.

If you use SAP Integration Suite (CPI), the switch is mostly a matter of configuration: you create an OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion credential and the adapter handles the rest. Manual testing in Postman has no equivalent built-in support. This post explains how to reproduce, step by step, what CPI does internally, using only Postman and OpenSSL.

The complete Postman collection, with all scripts in English, is attached to this post.

What you will be able to do

  • Generate your own RSA key pair and X.509 certificate.
  • Register an OAuth 2.0 client application in SAP SuccessFactors.
  • Build and digitally sign a SAML 2.0 assertion inside Postman, without any external tool.
  • Exchange the assertion for an OAuth access token and call the OData API.
  • Open an SFAPI session with the token and query CompoundEmployee over SOAP.

No prior OAuth or SAML knowledge is assumed. The explanations cover what happens at each step and why.

How it works

The method is the OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion grant. Instead of sending a password, you send SuccessFactors a short XML document, the assertion. The assertion states that the application with a given API Key is acting as a given user and that the request is valid for the next 10 minutes. You sign the assertion with a private key. SuccessFactors verifies the signature with the public certificate you registered earlier. If the signature matches, it returns an access token valid for about 24 hours, and you attach that token to every API call.

The setup has two parts:

  1. One-time setup: create a technical user with the right permissions, generate a key pair, register the certificate in an OAuth client in SuccessFactors, and create a Postman environment.
  2. Every session: generate the assertion, get the token, then call the OData API or open an SFAPI session and query CompoundEmployee.

Step A: Technical user and permissions

Create or reuse a dedicated technical user, for example API_TECH_USER, and assign a permission role that includes:

  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS OData API and Foundation OData API, for access to Employee Central entities.
  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS SOAP API, required for CompoundEmployee.
  • General User Permission → SFAPI User Login, required to open an SFAPI session.
  • The target population and field-level RBP. These define which employees and fields the API returns. If they are too narrow, you get empty results.

The permission Allow Admin to Access OData API through Basic Authentication is not needed for OAuth. Once the migration is complete, you can remove it to verify that nothing still depends on Basic Authentication.

Step B: Key pair and certificate

Generate a self-signed certificate and private key with OpenSSL:

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -sha256 -days 36500 -nodes \
  -keyout private.pem -out cert.pem -subj "/CN=postman-sf-ACMECORPT1"

Key points:

  • -nodes leaves the private key unencrypted. The Postman script needs an unencrypted PKCS#8 key.
  • The validity period is a decision to make together with the customer, in line with their security policy. A long validity avoids renewing the certificate and updating every Postman environment each year. A shorter lifetime reduces the impact if the key leaks. Either way, record the expiry date with openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -enddate.

SuccessFactors and the Postman variables need the Base64 content without the BEGIN/END lines and without line breaks. On Linux, macOS or Git Bash:

grep -v -- "-----" private.pem | tr -d '\n' > private_b64.txt
grep -v -- "-----" cert.pem    | tr -d '\n' > cert_b64.txt

On Windows PowerShell, use the equivalent Get-Content, Where-Object and Set-Content commands. The public certificate goes to SuccessFactors and to the Postman variable certificate_b64. The private key goes only into the Postman variable private_key_b64, and it must never be shared.

Step C: Register the OAuth client in SuccessFactors

In Admin Center, open Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and choose Register Client Application. Fill in:

  • Company: the tenant company ID (prefilled).
  • Application Name: free text. It appears in the token as issuedFor.
  • Application URL: used for identification only. No call is made to it.
  • Bind to Users: checked, and the technical user ID added. This restricts token issuance to the listed users and is recommended.
  • X.509 Certificate: paste the single-line Base64 certificate.

Do not click Generate X.509 Certificate. That creates a different key pair, and you already have yours. After registering, open the client and copy the API Key. It becomes the Postman variable client_id. The API Key is not a secret on its own, but it cannot be used to obtain tokens without the private key.

Step Postman environment

Create an environment, for example SF ACME Preview, with these variables:

Variable Content

urlThe API server of your data center, without a trailing slash. This is not the UI URL. Find it in SAP's list of SuccessFactors API servers.
userThe technical user ID from Step A. It goes into the assertion NameID.
companyThe tenant company ID.
client_idThe API Key of the OAuth client.
private_key_b64Content of private_b64.txt. Set the type to secret and fill only the Current value.
certificate_b64Content of cert_b64.txt. Optional, added to the assertion KeyInfo.
assertion, assertion_xml, sf_token, sf_token_exp, sessionIdLeft empty. They are written by the requests.

Postman keeps an Initial value and a Current value for each variable. Keep the private key, tokens and assertions in the Current value only, so they are not synced to the workspace or included in exports.

Collection structure

The collection can be run from top to bottom with the Collection Runner, or one request at a time:

  • SF SAML Bearer step by step
    1. Generate assertion: downloads the jsrsasign library and builds the signed assertion.
    2. Get token: exchanges the assertion for an access token.
    3. Call OData resource: calls the OData API with the Bearer token.
  • CompoundEmployee
    • Login CE: opens the SFAPI session.
    • GET CompoundEmployee: runs the SOAP query.
  • AllInOneCall (optional): a pre-request script that obtains a token automatically when needed.

Request 1: Generating the SAML assertion

SuccessFactors does not create the assertion for you. The old /oauth/idp endpoint is deprecated, because it required sending the private key over the network. So the assertion has to be built and signed on the client side. Postman's sandbox includes CryptoJS for hashing but no RSA signing, so the script first downloads jsrsasign, a pure JavaScript cryptography library.

The assertion contains:

  • ID and IssueInstant: a random identifier and the current UTC time.
  • Issuer: the fixed value www.successfactors.com.
  • Signature: an enveloped XML signature, placed right after the Issuer.
  • Subject / NameID: the technical user the API calls will run as.
  • SubjectConfirmationData: the Recipient is the /oauth/token endpoint.
  • Conditions: a validity window from 5 minutes in the past to 10 minutes in the future.
  • AttributeStatement: an api_key attribute with the client ID, which tells SuccessFactors which registered certificate to use.

The signature is produced in three steps. First, the assertion without the signature is hashed with SHA-256. Second, a small SignedInfo block describing the algorithms and the digest is assembled. Third, SignedInfo is signed with the private key using RSA-SHA256. SuccessFactors repeats the same computation with the registered certificate. If one byte differs, the verification fails.

One detail matters a lot: XML signatures are computed over a canonical form of the XML (Exclusive XML Canonicalization, exc-c14n). Postman has no canonicalization library, so the script writes the XML already in canonical form, with no spaces or line breaks between elements, attributes in alphabetical order and explicit closing tags. Do not reformat or indent the XML parts of the script. A single extra space breaks the signature.

Request 2: Getting the access token

The assertion is exchanged at {{url}}/oauth/token as an x-www-form-urlencoded body with four fields: client_id, company_id, grant_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer, and assertion. This must happen within the 10-minute window of the assertion.

The post-response script stores sf_token and an expiry timestamp. The expiry is set 5 minutes early to avoid using a token that expires in the middle of a call.

The token is Base64-encoded JSON. Decoding it is a useful sanity check, because it shows which API key and which user it was issued for.

Request 3: Calling the OData API

With the token, OData calls are simple: the token goes in the Authorization: Bearer header. For example:

  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/User?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/PerPerson?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/EmpJob?$filter=userId eq '100001'&$select=userId,startDate,company,department,jobCode&$format=json

To check whether a token is still valid, call {{url}}/oauth/validate with the Bearer token.

CompoundEmployee via SFAPI

CompoundEmployee is exposed by the SFAPI, the older SOAP API. Unlike OData, SFAPI works with sessions. A login operation returns a session ID, which is also set as the JSESSIONID cookie, and every query must carry that session.

The key finding from testing: sending the Bearer token directly on the query returns INVALID_SESSION. The token must first be used in a login call, and the login body must have empty companyId, username and password elements. If companyId or username are filled in, SuccessFactors attempts a classic password login and fails with FAILED_AUTHENTICATION. If the password element is removed altogether, the request fails schema validation. So the working combination is empty elements plus the Bearer header, which returns a session ID.

Then, for the query:

  • Set the cookie explicitly: Cookie: JSESSIONID={{sessionId}}.
  • Disable the Postman cookie jar, so that old session cookies are not sent.
  • Use a SOAP query with a SELECT on CompoundEmployee, for example on person, personal_information, employment_information and job_information.
  • For incremental extracts, add a delta filter such as WHERE last_modified_on > to_datetime('...'). Inside XML, the greater-than sign must be written as >.
  • When the response contains <hasMore>true</hasMore>, call queryMore with the returned querySessionId until hasMore is false.

The SFAPI session expires after 10 minutes of inactivity. If you get INVALID_SESSION, run the login again.

Lifetimes and run order

Item Lifetime When to regenerate

SAML assertion10 minutesRun Request 1 again if Request 2 is sent later than that.
Access tokenAbout 24 hoursRun Requests 1 and 2 again. The step-by-step flow does not refresh automatically.
SFAPI session10 minutes of inactivityRun Login CE again on INVALID_SESSION.
CertificateAs generated, or as agreed with the customerRotate before expiry: new key pair, then update the OAuth client and the Postman variables together.

A typical session is: generate the assertion, get the token, call OData as needed, log in to SFAPI, then run the CompoundEmployee query.

Troubleshooting

A few of the errors encountered while building this setup:

  • Identifier 't' has already been declared: the library was loaded in the same scope as the script. Load it with new Function(...), as the script does.
  • getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND undefined: a variable does not exist in the selected environment. Check the variable names and that the environment is selected.
  • Error from KEYUTIL.getKey: the key is not PKCS#8 or it is truncated. Regenerate it with -nodes, and check that the first line is -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.
  • /oauth/token rejects the assertion: the certificate registered in SuccessFactors does not match the key, the XML was altered, the clocks are out of sync, or the assertion is older than 10 minutes.
  • INVALID_SESSION on SOAP calls: the query was sent with the Bearer token instead of the session cookie, or an old cookie was sent. Log in first and disable the cookie jar.
  • FAILED_AUTHENTICATION on login: the credential elements were not empty, or the Bearer header was not set on the request.

Security

  • The private key is equivalent to the credentials of the technical user. Keep it only in the Postman Current value, marked as secret. Never commit it to a repository or share it in chats. Ideally, each colleague generates their own key pair and OAuth client.
  • Never send tokens to third-party hosts. The request that downloads the library from cdnjs must use No Auth. An inherited Bearer token would be sent to that host.
  • Use a dedicated technical user with minimal permissions and a restricted target population, and enable Bind to Users on the OAuth client.
  • Use separate key pairs and OAuth clients for each tenant, for example preview and production.
  • Once OAuth works, remove the Basic Authentication permission from the technical user.

Attached material

The attached Postman collection, OAuth Assertion - SuccessFactors, contains all the requests described above, in the order they should run, the complete Request 1 script, and the optional AllInOneCall request, which handles token renewal automatically.

Note: SAP Community does not accept .json attachments, so the collection is provided as a .txt file. Rename it to OAuth_Assertion_SuccessFactors.postman_collection.json before importing it into Postman. The file content is unchanged.

Before importing it, create the environment described in Step D. The collection contains no secrets. All tenant data in the examples (URLs, company ID, user, API key, keys and IDs) are fictitious, so replace them with your own tenant values.

I hope this helps anyone who needs to test SuccessFactors APIs from Postman without Basic Authentication. Questions and feedback are welcome in the comments

entry.title: From Integration to Intelligence :Building enterprise-ready AI agents with Integration Suite & MCP
entry.content:
I have sat through a lot of agent demos this year. The pattern is usually the same. Someone types a request in plain English, the agent reads a purchase requisition, checks a budget, creates a purchase order in S/4HANA, emails the supplier, and posts a cheerful summary. The room claps. It is impressive.

Then I ask the question that integration people always ask: what happens on the 40,000th run? What happens when the supplier endpoint times out, when the mapping changes, when audit wants to know who approved what, or when the token bill arrives at the end of the month?

That is the gap between an agent that works in a demo and an agent that survives production. After close to two decades of building integrations, first on Oracle SOA and OSB, later on Boomi, Apigee and SAP BTP, my view is that the gap is mostly not a model problem. It is an architecture problem. And it is one the SAP integration community is unusually well placed to solve.

Last week I attended SAP's session "Building the Autonomous Enterprise with Integration Suite, AEM, and Agents" (13 October 2026). One line from it has stayed with me, because it captures the whole argument in eight words:

"Let the agent think. Let Integration Suite execute."

This post is my attempt to unpack that line from an architect's point of view: where agents earn their keep, where they should stay out of the way, and how API-centric integration and the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite connect the two.

1. The overloaded agent

When teams first build agents, they tend to give them everything. The agent calls the APIs, builds the payloads, decides on retries, transforms the formats and handles the errors. It feels efficient because there is only one component to think about.

It is not efficient. In effect you are asking a probabilistic reasoning engine to re-implement things your integration platform already does deterministically, with monitoring, retries and audit built in. Mapping JSON to IDoc, routing a message by company code, validating mandatory fields against a schema, sending a payment file over a bank channel: none of these need judgment. They need to be done exactly the same way every time.

The SAP session framed the consequences well, and they match what I have seen in practice:

  • Duplicated capability. The agent rebuilds APIs, EDI handling, mappings and routing you already own.
  • Reduced reliability. Predictable PO, invoice and payment flows start to depend on non-deterministic behavior.
  • Harder governance. Security, auditability and compliance become difficult to standardize when logic lives inside prompts.
  • Blurred accountability. When something fails, is it the reasoning, the integration, the partner or the backend? Nobody can tell quickly.
  • Higher operating cost. Tokens and agent capacity are spent on repetitive plumbing instead of the reasoning you actually wanted.

I like to describe it as driving a Lamborghini to the supermarket. You can, but it is not what the car is for, and the parking is a nightmare.

2. Who should own each step? A Procure-to-Pay test

The most useful part of the session, for me, was a simple step-by-step assessment of a standard Procure-to-Pay flow. For each step, it asked one question: is the value here in reasoning, or in reliable execution? I have adapted it below because I think every team should run this exercise on its own processes before writing a single prompt.

#

P2P step

Agent value

Owner

Why

1

Medium

Agent

2

Approve requisition

High

Agent

Summarize context and policy, recommend

3

Create purchase order

Very high

Integration Suite

Structured execution: APIs, EDI, mapping

4

Very high

Integration Suite

Receive, transform, update

5

Very high

Very low

Integration Suite

6

Low

7

8

10
